book.bmfstown.horror.glow_lichen.name: Glow Lichen
book.bmfstown.horror.glow_lichen.ch1: Glow lichen had only ever grown on the stone walls of the mines underground. That morning it turned up beside the stone well at the centre of town. The grey-green flakes pressed flat into the cracks of the cobble, a faint cold light on their surface. I knocked a few off with a tool. When I came back that way at dusk, the bare stone was covered again in new growth.
book.bmfstown.horror.glow_lichen.ch2: By the next morning the whole street was covered in that grey-green film. It climbed the oak posts and the cobble walls, sealed over the glass windows, and lay across the roof planks, the crates indoors, even the beds. That night not a single torch was lit in the town, and the whole place still gave off a pale weak cold light.
book.bmfstown.horror.glow_lichen.ch3: The cattle and sheep in the pens had stopped moving too. Close up, the fleece had set into crusts, grey-green lichen pushing out of every seam, covering most of the eyes and ears. They stood there without moving, not even lowering their heads to graze.
book.bmfstown.horror.glow_lichen.ch4: Later the lichen reached the people of the town. At first only a few patches at hem and cuff, then it climbed the neck onto the face. Several of them stood at the corner of the street with half a face sealed in grey-green film, mouths slightly open, not making a sound.
book.bmfstown.horror.glow_lichen.ch5: Deeper into the town every wooden door stood open. The people inside stood straight up where they were, grey-green lichen pushing out through the eye sockets and nostrils, stretching the whole face out of shape. The mouths were packed with layer upon layer of fungal flake, growing down into the throat.
book.bmfstown.horror.glow_lichen.ch6: After dark the town was so quiet there was not a single footstep. Houses, soil, fences and the standing figures had all grown into one mass, wrapped under a thick grey-green coat, giving off an even faint light in the dark.
book.bmfstown.horror.eclipse.name: Eclipse
book.bmfstown.horror.eclipse.ch1: When the sun reached the top of the sky the light suddenly dropped a notch. I looked up: the edge of the square sun was missing a corner, as if something pure black had bitten it away. The lanterns lit themselves before their time, but the street stayed cold and dim.
book.bmfstown.horror.eclipse.ch2: Within moments only a thin white rim of the sun was left. The cattle and sheep that had been grazing stopped their mouths at the same instant, and there was no sound from the fish in the pond or the birds in the trees either. Every animal turned and lifted its head, staring straight up at the blackened sun.
book.bmfstown.horror.eclipse.ch3: The people walking in the street all stopped as well. The hammer at the forge hung in mid-air, the man at the well let go of his bucket. Everyone in the street stood where they were, necks bent at an unnatural angle, eyes fixed on the sky without blinking.
book.bmfstown.horror.eclipse.ch4: The last rim of white went out, and there was nothing in the sky but a pure black square ringed with a blinding white edge. Every torch and lantern flame went out and the town sank into a dead silent shadow. Except for the wind moving through the grass, nothing living made a sound. Everyone was still standing with their heads tipped back, motionless.
book.bmfstown.horror.eclipse.ch5: After a few minutes a white edge showed again at the rim of the black sun, and sunlight crept back over the ground. The water wheel turned again, the torches that had gone out lit again, and the animals and townsfolk frozen in place lowered their heads and went back to what they had been doing.
book.bmfstown.horror.eclipse.ch6: The day was fully bright again, as at any noon. People walked the street and worked with their heads down, the cattle and sheep went back to grazing, and no one looked up at the sky, and no one mentioned the few minutes it had gone dark, as if nothing had happened.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.name: The Order of the Stone
book.bmfstown.horror.man_in_fog.name: The Man in the Fog
book.bmfstown.horror.man_in_fog.ch1:
I was cutting wood at the edge of the woods on a foggy day, the view so short I couldn't make out the trunks further off. In the moment the fog opened a seam, a person was standing between two trees.
Same clothes as me, no name above him, perfectly still, facing this way. I took one step forward, the fog drifted across, and behind the trees there was nothing.
book.bmfstown.horror.man_in_fog.ch2:
I hadn't gone far into the woods when the ground suddenly opened up ahead. A dozen or so oaks stood there in neat rows, trunks perfectly fine, but not a single leaf left on any of the crowns -- as if someone had stripped them out block by block.
The leaves all around rustled in the wind. Those bare trunks did not move at all.
book.bmfstown.horror.man_in_fog.ch3:
Deep down the mine, the only sound in the whole tunnel was my pick striking stone. I looked off down the shaft, far into the black -- and away off there, two white points like eyes were faintly lit, staring straight back this way.
I waited. It didn't move, and it didn't go out. I didn't dare look that way again; I put the pick away and turned back.
book.bmfstown.horror.man_in_fog.ch4:
On the way back I turned into a side passage I'd never seen. The tunnel was cut dead straight -- plainly not a natural cave, and not a path I had dug either. Every few steps a redstone torch was set in the wall, the whole length of it.
The torches were burning with a dull red light, and yet they somehow lit hardly any ground at all; the stone around them stayed dim.
book.bmfstown.horror.man_in_fog.ch6:
Later I was in the house sorting a chest, doors and windows shut tight. As I bent over to put something away, my back suddenly went cold.
I was the only one in the whole house, and yet I knew perfectly well that right behind me, in the blind spot, less than a block from my back, someone was standing.
book.bmfstown.horror.man_in_fog.ch7:
The house was so quiet there wasn't a sound -- no footsteps, no door. I didn't dare put down what was in my hands, and I didn't dare turn around.
As long as I don't look back, as long as I keep my eyes on the chest in front of me, maybe I can go on pretending there's nothing behind me.
book.bmfstown.horror.woodcutter_hut.name: The Hut
book.bmfstown.horror.woodcutter_hut.ch1: Before dark I lost my way in the woods. The compass needle just kept turning in place. The cold came down fast. Far off between the trunks a shape of timber showed through, and close up it was an old wooden hut set deep in the trees. The door was not locked. The hinge creaked when I pushed it.
book.bmfstown.horror.woodcutter_hut.ch2: No lamp inside. By the faint light coming in through the doorway I could make out a wooden bed in the middle, a few bundles of firewood stacked in the corner. The hearth had gone cold long ago, and a thin layer of dust lay on the floor -- no footprints, no sign that anyone had lived here.
book.bmfstown.horror.woodcutter_hut.ch3: I barred the door, lay down, and looked around by the moonlight. All four wooden walls had a dozen or so portraits hung on them, evenly spaced, of different sizes, every frame dark. The faces in them were twisted and stiff, and every pair of eyes looked straight at the bed.
book.bmfstown.horror.woodcutter_hut.ch4: I turned over with my back to the wall and pulled the blanket over my head. There was not a breath of wind in the room, but the moment I closed my eyes I could feel those stares from all four walls still resting on my back, fixed on me, not moving.
book.bmfstown.horror.woodcutter_hut.ch5: I woke at first light. The room was much brighter than it had been in the night. I sat up and looked at the four walls again: the walls were bare, not one painting. Where the frames had hung the night before there were now rows of glass windows with no curtains drawn.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.ch1:
By the time night had fully settled, the chill of the mine shaft was still working its way up my trouser legs into my bones. With a heavy ore sack on my back I cut through the woods east of the village, and the sound of dry twigs snapping under my boots seemed unnaturally loud in the dark.
Not far from the path, on the trunk of an old oak, a light was leaking out that had no business being there. It was not a firefly, nor moonlight bent through the leaves: it seeped out of a square-cut gap in the bark itself. I got close. The wood there was a strange dark orange, covered in neat geometric latticework, with a slightly raised dot set in the middle.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.ch2:
Small yellow flecks winked in and out deep inside the lattice, with no pattern to them, and up close I could hear a very low, very steady hum, like some precise instrument running inside the trunk.
Without thinking I swung my steel pick with everything I had. No splinters flew. Not even a white mark was left. The point struck what felt like an invisible wall of absolute refusal; the ringing shock burst back up the handle and numbed my whole arm, splitting the web of my hand in one go. The thing never moved. It did not even miss a beat of its blinking.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.ch3:
And it was that one wild, uncontrolled swing that did it -- the loose sack on my shoulder lurched, and a lump of redstone ore, freshly chiselled out of a deep seam, slipped free and struck the bare root hard.
A clean cracking sound. Jolted by the impact, the crimson veins on the ore's face flared alight, like a lump of burning charcoal bursting open in the dark. It rolled away down the slope of the root and came to rest dead square against that patch of dark orange lattice on the trunk. The instant the red light touched the lattice, the hum rose sharply.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.ch4:
The world folded downward like a sheet of paper with its backing pulled away.
When I opened my eyes there was no night sky overhead and no soil underfoot. Up, down, left, right -- every inch I could see was packed with glowing blocks. Dark orange, deep violet, cold green: countless identical geometric lattices stretching away without end, woven into one enormous hive with no edge and no exit. A million faint lights crossed and flickered over each other, and the whole space pulsed with a low, orderly tremor, like the heart of something vast beating against my eardrum.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.ch5:
I lost my head completely and hacked at the block under my feet like a madman, and could not strike a single spark. I beat at it with my fists until my knuckles were a mess of blood, and the lights on those blocks did not change their flicker by the smallest fraction.
There were no doors, no seams, not even a way to tell which way was up, only an endless, indifferent array of instructions ticking over. They did not attack me and they did not answer me. They were dead things running on fixed rules, and they did not care in the least that a breathing man was now inside them.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.ch6:
The feeling of suffocation closed on my throat by degrees; the hum lay heavy and flat against my ears, and my thoughts were nearly ground to nothing by that dead, orderly stillness.
And then, when I could barely hold on any longer, the pulse of the whole space faltered -- the smallest possible hitch. It is hard to describe. It was like a set of precision gears, meshed tight and turning fast, suddenly noticing a speck of dust caught in the teeth, or a fly that had blundered in. No anger. No warning. The air went tight, and my sight was torn to pieces again.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.ch7:
Night wind poured back into my collar, and the damp smell of crushed grass hit my face.
I was still standing under that old tree, my sack spilled at my feet, the pick still locked in the stiff pose of a swing, and all of it had happened faster than a single heartbeat. Cold sweat ran down my temple. I gasped for air and told myself over and over: the thin air deep in the mine, the exhaustion, the nerves stretched tight in the dark -- they had put a moment of garish hallucination into my head. If I could just call it a trick of the eyes, everything could go back to the commonsense I knew.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.ch8:
Until my gaze slid slowly down to the redstone ore beside the root.
It had gone completely black. The stone's face was dull and cold, with not a trace of red left in it. When it had struck the root and lit up, that glow had been bright enough to show the blades of grass on the ground -- and anyone who has spent a lifetime down a mine knows perfectly well that redstone ore, once jolted alight, cannot go out between one blink and the next. It needs time. Tens of seconds of it. I had not been in that place for an instant.
book.bmfstown.horror.rocks_order.ch9:
I raised my head, shaking, and looked at the old oak again by moonlight. The trunk had gone back to ordinary rough bark. The dark orange lattice was gone without a trace, as though it had never been.
I picked up the cold lump of redstone and left the woods at something close to a run. But from that night on, whenever the world went quiet and I looked out of my window toward the woods east of the village, I could feel it: that low, regular hum, still coming through the thick timber, somewhere very deep in the world, beating on and on.
